column1: Spinoza — Substance, attribute, mode: define the three terms (E1D3-D5) and state how they lock together.
column2: Substance: what is in itself and is conceived through itself (E1D3) — its concept needs no other concept. Attribute: what the intellect perceives of substance as constituting its essence (E1D4) — for us, Thought and Extension. Mode: an affection of substance, what is in another and conceived through that other (E1D5) — this body, this idea. The lock: everything that exists is either substance or a mode of it, and each mode is conceived through the attribute it modifies — the whole ontology of the Ethics in three definitions.

column1: Spinoza — Deus sive Natura: state the claim 'God, or Nature,' and what it does and does not identify.
column2: Spinoza's phrase for the conclusion of Part I: God and Nature are one substance, not two realms (E1P14-P18, P29S). It identifies God with the total, self-caused, necessarily existing system — not with the mere sum of finite things: Nature as natura naturans (substance and its attributes) produces and contains natura naturata (all modes). God is the immanent, not transitive, cause of things. It does not identify God with this stone or that tree taken singly; each finite thing is a mode, divine only as an expression of the whole.

column1: Spinoza — Natura naturans / natura naturata: draw the distinction (E1P29S) and place three examples.
column2: E1P29S: by natura naturans, naturing Nature, understand what is in itself and conceived through itself — substance and its attributes, expressing God's eternal essence. By natura naturata, natured Nature, everything that follows from the necessity of God's nature — all the modes of the attributes. Examples of naturata: this body's motion, the idea of that body, the whole face of the universe of interrelated modes. The point: one Nature, two aspects — cause and effect internal to a single substance, not a creator standing outside a creation.

column1: Spinoza — Causa sui: define 'cause of itself' (E1D1), and explain why the notion is not a contradiction.
column2: E1D1: by cause of itself I understand that whose essence involves existence, or whose nature cannot be conceived except as existing. The apparent contradiction — a thing producing itself in time — dissolves once 'cause' is read as ground or reason, not temporal production: God's essence is such that nonexistence is inconceivable for it, the way a triangle's essence grounds its angles. It is the hinge of E1P7 (existence belongs to substance's nature) and E1P11 (God necessarily exists): only substance is causa sui; every mode has its cause in another.

column1: Spinoza — Adequate idea: define adequacy (E2D4), and distinguish it from bare truth.
column2: E2D4: an idea is adequate when, considered in itself, it has all the properties of a true idea — the mind is its adequate cause, understanding it through its causes rather than receiving it as a fragment of an affection. Truth concerns agreement with the object (extrinsic); adequacy concerns the idea's completeness within the mind (intrinsic): an adequate idea cannot be false (E2P34, P43). Inadequate ideas — imagination's fragments — are the seat of error and passion; therapy in Part V is the conversion of inadequate into adequate ideas.

column1: Spinoza — Substance monism: reconstruct the argument of E1P5, P11, and P14.
column2:
1. No two substances can share an attribute (E1P5): if they shared one, they could be told apart only by modes — but substance is prior to its modes (E1P1).
2. God, a substance of infinite attributes, necessarily exists (E1P11, via E1P7: existence belongs to substance's nature).
3. Therefore no substance besides God can be or be conceived (E1P14).
Objection: Leibniz: substances can be many, each conceived through itself in its own way.
Reply: their differentiating feature is then either an attribute (shared — excluded) or a mode (posterior — inadmissible).

column1: Spinoza — Necessary existence and universal necessity: reconstruct E1P11 with E1P29 and P33.
column2:
1. Existence belongs to the nature of substance (E1P7); God is substance consisting of infinite attributes (E1D6), so God necessarily exists (E1P11): a reason must be assignable for any thing's existence or nonexistence, and none can block God's.
2. Nothing in nature is contingent (E1P29): all follows from the necessity of the divine nature.
3. Things could not have been produced in any other manner or order (E1P33).
Objection: this collapses possibility into actuality and immunizes the system.
Reply: accepted as consequence: 'contingent' names only our ignorance of causes (E1P33S).

column1: Spinoza — The critique of teleology: reconstruct the Ethics I Appendix argument.
column2:
1. Humans act always on account of an end, and are conscious of their appetites while ignorant of the causes determining them.
2. Finding in nature many things serviceable to them — eyes for seeing, rain for crops — they infer that nature, and a ruler of nature, made all things for human use.
3. Setbacks are then explained as divine anger, and inquiry terminates in 'the will of God — the refuge of ignorance.'
4. But nature has no end set before it; final causes are human fictions.
Objection: explaining the belief's origin is not refuting it.
Reply: the refutation is E1P33; the Appendix explains why the error persists.

column1: Spinoza — Immanent cause: define the notion (E1P18) against transitive causation, and give its payoff.
column2: E1P18: God is the immanent, not the transitive, cause of all things. A transitive cause produces an effect outside itself, as a builder stands outside the house. An immanent cause's effect remains in the cause: modes are in God (E1P15) and conceived through God, as conclusions are in their premises. Payoff: no creation from nothing, no external craftsman, no intervention from outside nature — and no miracles in the vulgar sense, since nothing can enter the order from beyond it. It is Deus sive Natura stated causally, and the doctrine under the TTP's chapter on miracles.

column1: Spinoza — Eternity vs. duration: state the distinction (E1D8, E5) and its Part V use.
column2: Duration is indefinite continuation of existing — the mode's temporal career, measurable in before and after. Eternity, by E1D8, is existence itself insofar as it is conceived to follow necessarily from the definition of the eternal thing: not endless duration, but existence without reference to time at all. God is eternal; modes endure. Part V's middle path runs on the distinction: the mind is not immortal (it does not outlast the body in duration), yet something of it is eternal — an existence, as essence in God, to which duration does not apply.

column1: Spinoza — Parallelism: reconstruct E2P7 and its scholium.
column2:
1. From E1A4: knowledge of an effect depends on and involves knowledge of its cause.
2. Therefore the order and connection of ideas is the same as the order and connection of things (E2P7).
3. Scholium: a mode of Extension and its idea are one and the same thing, expressed in two ways.
So mind and body neither interact nor merely correspond: they are identical under two attributes.
Objection: the identity is asserted in the scholium, not proved — correspondence relabeled.
Reply: the proof is structural: attributes are conceived through themselves (E1P10), yet only one substance exists (E1P14) for both to express.

column1: Spinoza — The three kinds of knowledge: name and illustrate each (E2P40S2).
column2: First kind — imagination or opinion: ideas from random experience and signs, fragmentary and passive; the sun as a small disc two hundred feet away; the sole source of falsity. Second kind — reason: adequate ideas from common notions, what is equally in the part and in the whole; the sun's true structure and distance, proved. Third kind — scientia intuitiva: proceeding from an adequate idea of God's attributes to adequate knowledge of the essences of things, seeing each in its necessity at a single view. The ladder of the whole Ethics: bondage lives in the first kind, freedom in the second and third.

column1: Spinoza — Action and passion: state the definitions (E3D1-D3) and the Part V hinge.
column2: We act when something takes place, in us or outside us, of which we are the adequate cause — when it follows from our nature alone clearly understood (E3D1-D2). We are acted on, and suffer a passion, when we are only a partial cause: the effect outruns what our nature explains. Affects divide accordingly: passive affects rest on inadequate ideas; active affects — fortitude and nobility — on reason. Freedom is not exemption from causation but a shift in its address: more of what happens in you is action, less is passion. Part V's remedies are techniques for that shift.

column1: Spinoza — No free will: reconstruct E2P48 and the Letter 58 stone.
column2:
1. In the mind there is no absolute or free will: the mind is determined to will this or that by a cause, itself determined by another, to infinity (E2P48).
2. Will and intellect are one and the same (E2P49): volitions are just ideas' intrinsic affirmations, not a separate faculty's decrees.
3. Letter 58: a thrown stone, if conscious, would believe it flew of its own free will — conscious of its endeavor, ignorant of its causes; 'such is human freedom.'
Objection: deliberation is experienced as genuinely open.
Reply: the experience is real; the inference to causelessness is the stone's error.

column1: Spinoza — Conatus: reconstruct E3P6-P8.
column2:
1. Singular things are modes expressing God's power in a determinate way (E3P6 dem., from E1P25C, P34).
2. Nothing can be destroyed except by an external cause (E3P4); nothing in a thing's nature tends to its own destruction (E3P5).
3. Therefore each thing, insofar as it is in itself, strives (conatur) to persevere in its being (E3P6).
4. This striving is the thing's actual essence (E3P7), involving indefinite time (E3P8).
Objection: unfalsifiable — suicide and self-sacrifice get reassigned to external causes.
Reply: the reassignment is principled: self-destruction contradicts a mode's essence, so its explanation must lie outside it.

column1: Spinoza — The affects: define joy, sadness, and desire as the three primary affects (E3P11S).
column2: Desire is appetite conscious of itself — the conatus as it operates in a mind aware of its striving. Joy is the passion (or action) by which the mind passes to a greater perfection — an increase in the body's and mind's power of acting. Sadness is the passage to a lesser perfection — a decrease of that power. Every other affect is a compound: love is joy with the idea of an external cause; hate, sadness with such an idea; hope and fear, inconstant joy and sadness about a doubtful outcome. The triad is a physics of the soul: power rising, falling, or striving.

column1: Spinoza — Affect imitation: state E3P27 and its social consequences.
column2: E3P27: if we imagine a thing like us, toward which we have had no affect, to be affected with some affect, we are thereby affected with a like affect. Mechanism: the idea of a body resembling ours involves an affection resembling theirs. Consequences: pity, envy, emulation, and ambition are contagious by structure, not by choice; crowds synchronize; we strive that others love what we love (E3P31) — making affective life inherently social. It is the transmission belt from Part III's psychology to the Political Treatise's multitude: politics is imitation, managed or unmanaged.

column1: Spinoza — Hope and fear: give Spinoza's definitions and their political load.
column2: E3, Definitions of the Affects XII-XIII: hope is an inconstant joy, born of the image of a future or past thing whose outcome we doubt; fear is an inconstant sadness from the same doubtful image. While doubt stands, hope and fear imply each other (E3P50S). Their instability makes them the governing passions of unreason: the TTP's Preface argues that fear is the engine of superstition, and rulers who govern by managed hope and fear keep the multitude in bondage. A mind that understands causes swaps both for a steadier joy — which is why the affects are a political science.

column1: Spinoza — Good and evil as modes of thinking: reconstruct the Ethics IV Preface argument.
column2:
1. Perfection and imperfection, good and evil, indicate nothing positive in things considered in themselves: the same music is good for the melancholy man, bad for the mourner, neither for the deaf (E4 Preface).
2. We judge things against a model of human nature we set before ourselves: good as they approach it, evil as they fall short.
3. Retained, redefined: good = what we certainly know to be useful to us; evil = what we certainly know hinders us (E4D1-D2).
Objection: this dissolves normativity into preference.
Reply: usefulness is objective relative to human nature: what increases power of acting is good for any human, whether felt or not.

column1: Spinoza — Bondage and the remedies: reconstruct Part IV's diagnosis with Part V's cures.
column2:
Bondage is the human lack of power to moderate the affects: passive affects rest on inadequate ideas and can overpower knowledge (E4P1-P17). The cures are cognitive and causal, not volitional (E5P20S): know the affect itself; separate it from the thought of an external cause; let time weaken imagined objects; multiply the causes sustaining good affects; order thoughts by understanding necessity. An affect ceases to be a passion as soon as we form a clear idea of it (E5P3).
Objection: therapy by understanding seems too weak against addiction and grief.
Reply: nothing stronger exists: an affect is restrained only by a stronger affect (E4P7) — understanding works by generating one.

column1: Spinoza — Virtue = power: state E4D8 and what the identity changes.
column2: E4D8: by virtue and power I understand the same thing — virtue, insofar as it is related to man, is man's very essence or nature insofar as he has the power of bringing about what can be understood through the laws of his nature alone. The identity abolishes the gap between moral worth and efficacy: a virtuous act is not one that obeys an external rule but one that flows from one's own nature adequately understood — action rather than passion, at the level of character. Ethics becomes a branch of the physics of power.

column1: Spinoza — The dictates of reason: state E4P18S's demands and their ground.
column2: E4P18S: reason demands nothing contrary to nature; it demands that everyone love himself, seek his own advantage — what is really useful to him — desire what leads to greater perfection, and strive to preserve his being. From this ground, not from any command, follow the social theorems: nothing is more useful to man than man (E4P35C); men agree in nature insofar as they live by reason (E4P35); the good each rational person seeks for himself he desires for others, and the more, the more he knows God (E4P37). Self-interest so understood that it entails community.

column1: Spinoza — The free man: state the model of E4P67-P73 and its point.
column2: The free man is Part IV's regulative model: one who lives according to the dictate of reason alone. He thinks of nothing less than of death; his wisdom is a meditation on life (E4P67). He is more free in a state, living by common decision, than in solitude (E4P73); he avoids dangers by reason rather than fear, acts honestly, and seeks the company of other free people. The model's point is measured honesty: humans are necessarily partly passive (E4P4C) — the free man is not a description but a compass heading, fixing what 'more free' means as bondage decreases.

column1: Spinoza — Intellectual love of God and the eternity of the mind: reconstruct E5P23-P42 with the scholarly dispute flagged.
column2:
1. From knowledge of the third kind arises the intellectual love of God — joy with the idea of God as cause (E5P32C-P33).
2. This love is eternal, and it is God's own love of himself insofar as expressed through the human mind (E5P36).
3. The human mind cannot be absolutely destroyed with the body: something of it remains which is eternal (E5P23) — though memory and imagination perish (E5P21, P34).
4. Blessedness is not the reward of virtue, but virtue itself (E5P42).
Dispute (unresolved): what the 'eternal part' is — timeless essence, experienced timelessness, or a doctrine in tension with P21 — remains contested; the dossier takes no side.

column1: Spinoza — Amor Dei intellectualis: define the intellectual love of God without personalizing it.
column2: The affect at the summit of Part V: joy accompanied by the idea of God as its cause, arising not from imagination or reason's general truths but from the third kind of knowledge (E5P32C). It is not devotion to a person: God is without passions and is affected by no joy or sadness (E5P17), so this love asks nothing back — whoever loves God cannot strive that God love him in return (E5P19). Reflexively, it is God's love of himself insofar as he is expressed through the human mind (E5P36). Its felt character is acquiescentia: contentment in seeing all things in their necessity.

column1: Spinoza — Beatitudo: state what blessedness is, and what it is not (E5P42).
column2: Blessedness (beatitudo) is Spinoza's word for the final state the Ethics aims at: the mind's perfection in the intellectual love of God. E5P42 states its paradox: blessedness is not the reward of virtue, but virtue itself — we do not restrain our lusts and enjoy blessedness as payment; it is because we enjoy blessedness that we are able to restrain them. The order is anti-Kantian: morality is not self-conquest compensated later, but power itself, experienced as joy. Nor is it a state after death: it names a quality of this life, available insofar as the mind knows adequately.

column1: Spinoza — Against Descartes' pineal interaction: reconstruct the E5 Preface critique.
column2:
1. Descartes seated the soul's control of the body in the pineal gland, a small mid-brain organ he supposed uniquely mobile, where mind and animal spirits move each other.
2. E5 Preface: a hypothesis more occult than any occult quality — no mechanism, no measure, no explanation of how an unextended thing moves an extended one.
3. He adds a will of absolute dominion over the affects — refuted daily, since men know the better and do the worse.
Objection: Descartes had the science of his day; the mockery is cheap.
Reply: the charge is structural: interaction relabeled where cross-attribute causation is impossible (E2P6); parallelism is the alternative.

column1: Spinoza — Sub specie aeternitatis: define 'under a species of eternity' and its cognitive role.
column2: To conceive a thing sub specie aeternitatis is to conceive it through God's essence — as following necessarily from the divine nature, without relation to a particular time and place (E2P44C2; E5P29). It is the stance of the second and especially the third kind of knowledge, opposed to imagination's view of things as present, dated, and contingent. Its role is epistemic and therapeutic at once: what is understood under a species of eternity is understood adequately, and adequate understanding is what converts passions into actions. The phrase is Spinoza's shortest formula for the whole method.

column1: Spinoza — The TTP's separation of theology and philosophy: reconstruct chs. 14-15 and 20.
column2:
1. Scripture's teaching reduces to obedience — justice and charity; its seven dogmas of universal faith need only be pious, not true (TTP ch. 14).
2. Theology and philosophy therefore govern separate domains: neither is the handmaid of the other (ch. 15); reason is censored by no doctrine, and Scripture teaches no metaphysics.
3. Granting freedom to philosophize costs a state neither piety nor peace; suppressing judgment breeds flattery and sedition (ch. 20).
4. Conclusion: the true aim of government is liberty.
Objection: the 'obedience only' reading flattens Scripture's cognitive claims.
Reply: the hermeneutics of chs. 1-7 yield it: Scripture speaks in its audience's idiom, not in concepts.

column1: Spinoza — Right = power and democracy: reconstruct TTP ch. 16 with the Political Treatise.
column2:
1. In the state of nature, each thing's right extends exactly as far as its power: the big fish eat the small by sovereign natural right (TTP ch. 16; TP ch. 2).
2. A contract transfers no right beyond the power surrendered; sovereignty endures only while the multitude's power sustains it.
3. Democracy keeps right where power already lies: the most natural regime, closest to nature's freedom (TP ch. 11, unfinished).
Objection: right reduced to power destroys normativity — might makes right.
Reply: it grounds normativity where it can operate: institutions are judged by how they channel the multitude's power.

column1: Spinoza — Superstition: state the TTP Preface's account of its cause and use.
column2: The TTP's Preface: men are prone to superstition when governed by fear — fortune's uncertainty swings them between hope and dread, and in distress they read omens, credit prophets, and surrender judgment to whoever promises control. Superstition is therefore not stupidity but an affect with causes, and it is politically useful: maintained by fear, it makes minds governable, so rulers and clergy who monopolize its interpretation hold a second sovereignty. Its cure is the same as Part V's: understand the causes — of fortune's swings, of one's fear, of the institutions farming both — and the omens lose their market.

column1: Spinoza — Miracles: state the TTP ch. 6 critique and its metaphysical root.
column2: TTP ch. 6: a miracle, properly, would be an event contrary to nature's fixed and immutable order. But that order is God's decrees themselves (E1P29, P33): an event against it would be God acting against himself. What are called miracles are events whose natural causes the narrator and audience do not know — Scripture recounts them in the idiom and opinions of their time. The argument's strength is its root: not induction from science but deduction from the metaphysics — God's will is not a king's, issuing exceptions. Its exposure is the same root: it stands or falls with Part I.

column1: Spinoza — Prophecy and imagination: state the TTP chs. 1-2 doctrine.
column2: TTP chs. 1-2: prophecy is certain knowledge revealed by God to men — but its certainty is moral, not mathematical, and its medium is imagination: the prophets excelled in vivid imagination and in virtue, not in intellect; their revelations were adapted to their own opinions and era (a prophet ignorant of astronomy received the sun as standing still). Hence Scripture's authority covers conduct, not cosmology or metaphysics; its authors are authorities on justice and charity, not on nature. The doctrine founds the separation thesis: prophecy, being imagination perfected by morality, cannot make philosophy its handmaid, nor be made philosophy's.
